# Calibration: what the shipped TxGraffiti filters discard on `graph_data`

Every number below is filled in from `results/rows/` by `docs/gen/render.py`.
Status: internal calibration for Project B, not a publication. Ján Pastorek and Randy Davila were
written to in October 2026 about the points below that concern their code. Where they have not
answered, those points are our reading and measurement of their code, and may be wrong.

## Scope and pinning

- System measured: the `txgraffiti` package, version 0.4.1, called unmodified.
  Not the paper's abstract design, and not the website.
- Table: shipped `graph_data`, 340 objects, sha256 `d074e50dac28…`.
- Target `independence_number`; all 23 other numeric columns as features (`feature_size` one);
  all 13 boolean columns as hypotheses.
- Generators in `txgraffiti2`'s default order: `linear_programming`, `convex_hull`, `ratios`. Candidates per generator: `linear_programming` 598, `convex_hull` 1348, `ratios` 598.
  LP runs on PuLP's bundled CBC, put on PATH because the package's solver lookup did not find it
  on our machine (gate G-A0).
- Seed 0; chance baselines use 1000 draws.

Pool: 2544 generated, `remove_duplicates` removes 828 (32.5%), leaving
**1716 candidates**. Of these, 244 are false on the table, 1641 are distinct
on the table, and they span 13 hypotheses.

## 1. Three-way partition, each rule separately on the same pool

The package's filters return lists, so they do not produce the paper's alias class.
Here a rejected candidate is an **alias** when an accepted candidate is identical to it
on the table (same lhs, operator, hypothesis rows and right-hand values there);
every other rejection is **discarded**. The definition is ours, not txgraffiti's.

| rule (shipped code) | input | representative | alias | discarded | discarded & false | killed | wall s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `filter_with_dalmatian` (heuristics.fajtlowicz) | 1716 | 779 | 14 | 923 | 244 | 937 (54.6%) | 46.488 |
| `sophie_accept`, greedy (heuristics.delavina) | 1716 | 1 | 0 | 1715 | 244 | 1715 (99.9%) | 0.361 |
| `filter_with_morgan` (heuristics.davila) | 1716 | 830 | 17 | 869 | 111 | 886 (51.6%) | 0.181 |

`sophie_accept` has no shipped filter wrapper; it is driven greedily in pool order
against the previously accepted list, as its docstring describes. It only looks at
hypothesis coverage. On this table it accepts 1: the first candidate in the pool has
hypothesis `connected`, which holds on every object, so nothing after it adds coverage.
Its kill rate records a mismatch of purpose (Sophie was designed for sufficient conditions,
not for bounds under single-predicate hypotheses), not a flaw.

**Dalmatian by operator.** Upper bounds: 942 in the pool (781 true on the table),
88 accepted, 693 true ones rejected. Lower bounds: 774 in the pool
(691 true), 691 accepted, 0 true ones rejected,
so on this table Dalmatian filters lower bounds by validity alone. The cause is in the source: `dalmatian_accept` collects only `<=` bounds as
existing bounds, so a true `>=` candidate is compared against upper bounds, whose row-wise minimum
it lies below almost everywhere. Of Dalmatian's 779 representatives, 691
are lower bounds.

Further detail: 0 accepted candidates had no competing upper bound in their group;
21 rested on a single strictly-below row; 336 objects
witness all strict acceptances.

## 2. Object-database floor

For every decision and every object, would the shipped rule decide differently if that
one object were removed (candidate pool held fixed)? Computed by kernels that match the
shipped rule exactly on the full table, on sampled removals (G-A4), and on every removal
of a small table (`tests/test_rules.py`).

| rule | fragile decisions | fragile & accepted | fragile & rejected | objects with a flip | objects for 50% / 90% of flips | top objects: flips |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `filter_with_dalmatian` (heuristics.fajtlowicz) | 50 (2.9%) | 21 | 29 | 24 | 6 / 19 | row 171 (n=8, m=16): 7, row 102 (n=18, m=27): 5, row 82 (n=14, m=13): 4, row 286 (n=2, m=1): 4, row 144 (n=12, m=30): 3 |
| `sophie_accept`, greedy (heuristics.delavina) | 0 (0.0%) | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 / 0 | none |
| `filter_with_morgan` (heuristics.davila) | 5 (0.3%) | 5 | 0 | 1 | 1 / 1 | row 77 (n=4, m=6): 5 |

Reading: a decision is **fragile** when removing a single object flips it. Only single-object
removals are measured; decisions that need two objects removed together are not counted.

## 3. Chance baseline

A random rule accepts the same number of candidates, uniformly. "P(random ≥ rule)" is the
share of draws that match or beat the rule on that metric.

| rule | accepted (k) | metric | rule | random mean [2.5%, 97.5%] | P(random ≥ rule) | reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `filter_with_dalmatian` (heuristics.fajtlowicz) | 779 | objects with a tight survivor | 248 | 245.03 [231.975, 252] | 0.382 | inside the random 95% range |
| `filter_with_dalmatian` (heuristics.fajtlowicz) | 779 | false conjectures kept | 0 | 110.89 [95, 125] | 1.0 | below the random 95% range |
| `filter_with_dalmatian` (heuristics.fajtlowicz) | 779 | hypotheses kept | 13 | 13.0 [13, 13] | 1.0 | inside the random 95% range |
| `filter_with_dalmatian` (heuristics.fajtlowicz) | 779 | distinct table classes kept | 746 | 761.39 [754, 768] | 1.0 | below the random 95% range |
| `sophie_accept`, greedy (heuristics.delavina) | 1 | objects with a tight survivor | 16 | 3.65 [0, 21] | 0.051 | inside the random 95% range |
| `sophie_accept`, greedy (heuristics.delavina) | 1 | false conjectures kept | 0 | 0.15 [0, 1] | 1.0 | inside the random 95% range |
| `sophie_accept`, greedy (heuristics.delavina) | 1 | hypotheses kept | 1 | 1.0 [1, 1] | 1.0 | inside the random 95% range |
| `sophie_accept`, greedy (heuristics.delavina) | 1 | distinct table classes kept | 1 | 1.0 [1, 1] | 1.0 | inside the random 95% range |
| `filter_with_morgan` (heuristics.davila) | 830 | objects with a tight survivor | 253 | 246.32 [237, 252] | 0.007 | above the random 95% range |
| `filter_with_morgan` (heuristics.davila) | 830 | false conjectures kept | 132 | 118.12 [103, 132] | 0.026 | inside the random 95% range |
| `filter_with_morgan` (heuristics.davila) | 830 | hypotheses kept | 13 | 13.0 [13, 13] | 1.0 | inside the random 95% range |
| `filter_with_morgan` (heuristics.davila) | 830 | distinct table classes kept | 805 | 810.26 [803, 817] | 0.938 | inside the random 95% range |

Reading for Dalmatian, the headline rule: it keeps no false conjecture (random draws keep many), but on
the two redundancy metrics it is inside the random 95% range for objects with a tight survivor and
below the random 95% range for distinct table classes. Morgan is
above the random 95% range for tight objects. A kill rate says nothing until it is read against these ranges.

## 4. AutoGraphForge's known-results filter (the other kind of filter)

Credit: Ján Pastorek, AutoGraphForge (commit `510cf50`). This is a novelty filter,
not a redundancy filter; its counts are never added to the numbers above.

**On the TxGraffiti pool.** TxGraffiti writes `(hyp) → (body)`; AutoGraphForge's parser needs `⇒`.
The arrow swap is the only adapter, and the unadapted run is kept as a control.

| verdict set | columns | errors | known in pool | known in pipeline survivors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| arrow adapter, table columns | 37 | 0 | 132 (7.7%) | 14 (3.7%) |
| arrow adapter, _GC2TABLE columns | 44 | 0 | 115 (6.7%) | 9 (2.4%) |
| no adapter, table columns | 37 | 0 | 0 (0.0%) | 0 (0.0%) |

**On AutoGraphForge's own CEGIS output** (6522 statements): the standalone call with the
module's `_GC2TABLE` columns flags 154; the verdicts the pipeline stored flag
33; 8 are in both, 146 only standalone, 25 only stored.
The difference follows the column list passed to the same function. Which list the pipeline
intends is a question we put to the author; until he answers, this is our reading of his code. The earlier report's
"novel survivors equal survivors" holds by construction (survivors were filtered to novel first)
and is not a kill count.

## What this calibration says for Project B

- Report each rule's partition separately and with its own chance baseline; a kill rate alone
  does not show whether a rule keeps anything a random rule would not.
- Emit per-object flip counts: they show how much each accept/reject decision rests on single objects.
- Name the column list and the statement syntax for any novelty verdict.
- A generator that fails silently must be an error, not zero candidates.
